title: Yhdeksän vuoden polku on takana
subtitle: Your son's graduation — real Finnish from a real day

blocks.text: Today your son finished peruskoulun — Finland's nine-year basic education. The speeches you heard were real, unscripted Finnish: a class supervisor's farewell, student words, the texture of a Finnish school ceremony. This lesson turns that day into language. Every phrase here was said in that room.

blocks.title: What just happened — the Finnish school system
blocks.text: Peruskoulu (basic school) runs from age 7 to 16 — grades 1 through 9. Grades 1–6 are alakoulu (lower school), grades 7–9 are yläkoulu (upper school). Finishing grade 9 is a genuine milestone: after this, students choose between lukio (upper secondary / academic path), ammattikoulu (vocational school), or opisto (college/institute). The todistus (certificate) they receive today opens those doors.
The opening — Tämä on suuri päivä

blocks.annotated: {Tämä|word|pronoun|this (formal)} on {suuri|word|adjective|big/great} {päivä|word|noun|day}. Yksi {merkittävä|word|adjective|significant/important} {luku|word|noun|chapter} {elämässänne|phrase|inessive plural|in your lives} tulee {päätökseen|phrase|illative|to an end/conclusion}.
blocks.translation: This is a big day. A significant chapter in your lives is coming to an end.

blocks.title: Elämässänne — inside your lives
blocks.text: Elämä (life) → elämässä (in life, inessive case: -ssä = inside) → elämässänne (in your lives, with -nne = your plural possessive suffix). Finnish stacks meaning onto one word: elämä + ssä + nne = in-your-lives. You heard this in the speech as one flowing word. This is Finnish case + possessive suffix working together.

blocks.translation: Nine years of primary school are behind you.

blocks.title: Peruskoulupolku — compound word of the day
blocks.text: Peruskoulu (basic school) + polku (path/trail) = peruskoulupolku. The school journey as a literal forest path — a very Finnish metaphor. Polku appears constantly in Finnish speeches, graduations and poetry as a metaphor for life's journey. On takana (is behind) is the elegant Finnish way of saying 'we've done it, it's in the past.'
The journey metaphor — Matkaan on mahtunut

blocks.annotated: {Matkaan|word|illative|into the journey} on {mahtunut|grammar|perfect passive|has fitted/included} {valtavasti|word|adverb|enormously/a huge amount}.
blocks.translation: The journey has included an enormous amount.

blocks.title: Matkaan on mahtunut — a beautifully Finnish construction
blocks.text: Mahtua means 'to fit into.' Matkaan on mahtunut literally means 'into the journey has fitted' — as if the journey is a bag and life's experiences are packed into it. It's passive perfect: something fitted itself in. You'll hear matkaan on mahtunut at every Finnish graduation. It's the standard ceremonial phrase for 'a lot has happened along the way.'

items.en: The journey has included great experiences.

blocks.text: The you-have-grown section — Finnish perfect tense

blocks.annotated: Te {olette|grammar|perfect auxiliary|have (plural)} {kasvaneet|grammar|past participle|grown}. Olette {oppineet|grammar|past participle|learned} uusia {taitoja|word|partitive plural|skills}. Olette {löytäneet|grammar|past participle|found/discovered} omia {vahvuuksiaan|phrase|partitive possessive|their own strengths}.
blocks.translation: You have grown. You have learned new skills. You have found your own strengths.

blocks.title: Olette + past participle — Finnish present perfect
blocks.text: From Lesson 5 you learned olen ollut (I have been). Now: olette kasvaneet (you plural have grown), olette oppineet (you have learned), olette löytäneet (you have found). The pattern is: olla conjugated (olen/olet/on/olette) + past participle ending in -nut/-nyt/-neet. This is the most important tense in Finnish ceremony and formal speech.
Resilience — a very Finnish word appears

blocks.translation: These all build resilience — that celebrated resilience.

blocks.title: Sitkeys vs resilienssi — and Finnish sisu
blocks.text: Sitkeys (tenacity, grit, stick-to-it-ness) is a deep Finnish word. Resilienssi is the modern loanword from English. The speaker uses both — and the phrase sitä kuuluisaa (that famous/celebrated) is gently ironic: everyone knows resilience is important, it's become almost a cliché in Finnish education speech. Sitkeys is related to sisu — the untranslatable Finnish concept of inner determination. Your son learned both today.
The imperatives — commands of encouragement

blocks.title: Finnish imperative plural — Muistakaa, Uskokaa, Olkaa
blocks.text: When speaking to a group in Finnish, the imperative (command/encouragement) adds -kaa/-kää to the verb stem. You, remember! = Muistakaa! You, believe! = Uskokaa! You, be! = Olkaa! You, head/direct yourselves! = Suunnatkaa! This is the grammar of graduation speeches, coaches, teachers, and leaders. Every -kaa/-kää you hear is someone rallying a group.

items.en: Remember the first day of school.
Believe in yourselves and your own possibilities.
Head boldly. / Go forth with courage.

blocks.text: The path ahead — lukio, ammattikoulu, opisto

blocks.annotated: {Jokaisen|word|genitive|each person's} teidän {polkunne|phrase|possessive|your path} on {arvokas|word|adjective|valuable/worthy}, {valitsettepa|grammar|concessive|whether you choose} {lukion|word|accusative|upper secondary}, {ammattikoulun|word|accusative|vocational school} tai {opiston|word|accusative|college/institute}.
blocks.translation: Each of your paths is valuable, whether you choose upper secondary, vocational school, or college.

blocks.text: The thanks — Lämmin kiitos

blocks.annotated: {Lämmin|word|adjective|warm} {kiitos|word|noun|thank you} {huoltajille|word|allative plural|to the guardians/parents} {tuesta|word|elative|for the support}, {herätyksistä|word|elative plural|for the wake-up calls} ja {myötäelämisestä|phrase|elative|for the compassion/empathy}.
blocks.translation: Warm thanks to the parents for the support, the wake-up calls, and the compassion.

blocks.title: Myötäeläminen — living alongside someone
blocks.text: Myötä = along with / in the same direction. Eläminen = living. Myötäeläminen = living alongside someone in their experience, feeling what they feel. It's empathy expressed as a shared journey. There is no single English word for it. The -elä root (to live) is everywhere in Finnish: elämä (life), elää (to live), myötäelää (to co-experience). This is one of the most beautiful words in the language.

blocks.annotated: Te {olette kulkeneet|grammar|perfect|have walked} tämän matkan näiden nuorten {rinnalla|word|adessive|alongside / by the side of}.
blocks.translation: You have walked this journey alongside these young people.

blocks.title: Rinnalla — beside, at the side of
blocks.text: Rinta = chest / side. Rinnalla = at the side of / alongside. Kulkea rinnalla (to walk alongside) is the Finnish image of parenting, friendship, and mentorship. Not leading from the front, not pushing from behind — walking beside. You walked rinnalla today.
The student speech — Yhteisöllisyys

blocks.annotated: {Yhteisöllisyys|phrase|compound noun|community spirit / sense of togetherness} {näkyy|word|verb|is visible/shows} erityisesti {koulutapahtumissa|word|inessive plural|in school events}.
blocks.translation: Community spirit shows especially in school events.

blocks.title: Yhteisöllisyys — the word Finnish schools live by
blocks.text: Yhteisö (community) + llisyys (abstract noun suffix) = yhteisöllisyys. The quality of being a community, of belonging together. Finnish schools are evaluated on it. It's the opposite of individualism — the sense that the group looks after itself. You cannot translate it in one word: 'community spirit,' 'sense of togetherness,' 'collective belonging' all get part of it.

blocks.translation: We wouldn't have survived without them.

blocks.title: Emme olisi selvinneet — conditional perfect
blocks.text: Selvitä = to survive / to manage / to get through. Emme olisi selvinneet = we would not have survived. This is conditional perfect: emme (we not) + olisi (would have) + selvinneet (survived). From Lesson 7 you saw olisin voinut (I could have been). Same pattern: olisi + past participle. It's the tense of things that didn't happen — regret, relief, gratitude.
The closing words

blocks.annotated: {Toivotan|word|verb|I wish} teille {jokaiselle|word|allative|to each of you} {onnea|word|partitive|happiness/luck} ja {menestystä|word|partitive|success}. {Oikein|word|adverb|really/truly} {hyvää|word|partitive|good} {kesää|word|partitive|summer}!
blocks.translation: I wish each of you happiness and success. Have a truly good summer!

blocks.title: Hyvää kesää — the Finnish farewell of summer
blocks.text: From May onwards, every Finnish goodbye includes hyvää kesää (good summer, partitive). It's not just polite — Finnish summer is genuinely precious after a long dark winter. When a Finnish teacher says hyvää kesää at a graduation, they mean it with full weight. You heard it today. Now you can say it back.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Congratulations! Nine years are behind you.

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Kiitos! Matkaan on mahtunut niin paljon.
lines.en: Thank you! The journey has included so much.

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: I'm applying to upper secondary. I'm excited.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fi: Hienoa! Uskokaa itseänne. Oikein hyvää kesää!
lines.en: Wonderful! Believe in yourself. Have a truly good summer!

blocks.title: Onnittelut — the word you needed today
blocks.text: Onnittelut = congratulations (from onnitella = to congratulate). The single most useful word you could have used today. If you said it to your son's teacher or classmates, you said something real. If you didn't — you know it now.

blocks.content: Yhteisöllisyys: YH-tei-söl-li-syys (six syllables — take it slowly). Myötäeläminen: MYÖTÄ-e-lä-mi-nen (myötä rhymes with 'quota' said softly). Sitkeys: SIT-keys (sit + kays, hard k). Peruskoulupolku: PE-rus-kou-lu-pol-ku (seven clean syllables, stress always on first).
